abstract: Post-translational modifications of tubulin diversify microtubule function by generating distinct molecular states collectively known as the tubulin code. Whereas the reversible tyrosination cycle is a conserved feature of -tubulin throughout eukaryotes, in trypanosomatid parasites, {beta}-tubulin also carries a genetically encoded C-terminal tyrosine, which is subjected to detyrosination and whose biological role remains unknown. Here, we show that {beta}-tubulin tyrosination is rare across eukaryotes but highly conserved across trypanosomatids. Using genome editing to uncouple the tyrosination states of - and {beta}-tubulin in Trypanosoma brucei, we demonstrate that the {beta}-tubulin C-terminal tyrosine independently contributes to the regulation of microtubule glutamylation. Rather than depending on - or {beta}-tubulin alone, glutamylation levels reflect the combined tyrosination states of both subunits. Strikingly, either increasing or reducing {beta}-tubulin tyrosination produces opposing changes in parasite morphometry, single-cell motility and collective migration. Together, these findings establish {beta}-tubulin (de)tyrosination as an evolutionarily conserved component of the trypanosomatid tubulin code that contributes to microtubule regulation and function in T. brucei, extending the significance of tubulin tyrosination beyond the canonical -tubulin tyrosination cycle.
